content: Attachment measures are tools and procedures used to evaluate attachment patterns in both children and adults. Researchers have developed various methods to assess attachment in children, such as the Strange Situation procedure and story-based approaches like the Attachment Story Completion Test. These methods classify children into four attachment styles: secure, anxious-ambivalent, anxious-avoidant, and disordered. In adults, attachment is commonly measured using the Adult Attachment Interview (AAI) and self-report questionnaires. Self-report questionnaires identify two dimensions of attachment: anxiety about the relationship and avoidance in the relationship. These dimensions define four adult attachment styles: secure, preoccupied, dismissive-avoidant, and fearful-avoidant. Measuring Attachment in Children Researchers have devised several methods to assess attachment in children. One of the most well-known is the Strange Situation, developed by developmental psychologist Mary Ainsworth. This procedure observes the attachment relationship between a caregiver and a child. During the Strange Situation, the child is observed playing for 20 minutes while caregivers and strangers enter and leave the room, simulating the presence and absence of familiar and unfamiliar individuals in the child’s life. The situation varies in stressfulness, and the child’s responses are carefully observed. The child experiences the following scenarios: 1. The mother and baby enter the room. 2. The mother sits quietly on a chair, responding if the infant seeks attention. 3. A stranger enters, talks to the mother, and gradually approaches the infant with a toy. The mother leaves the room. 4. The stranger leaves the infant playing unless the infant becomes inactive, in which case the stranger tries to engage the infant with toys. If the infant becomes distressed, this episode ends. 5. The mother re-enters and waits to see how the infant greets her. The stranger leaves quietly, and the mother waits until the baby settles before leaving again. 6. The infant is left alone. This episode is curtailed if the infant appears distressed. 7. The stranger returns and repeats the earlier interaction. 8. The mother returns, and the stranger leaves. Reunion behavior is noted, and the situation ends. The child’s reactions to the caregiver’s departure and return, as well as their engagement with new toys, are observed throughout the procedure. Other Approaches Narrative and story-based methods are often used with older toddlers, children, and teens to assess their state of mind regarding attachment. One such method is the Attachment Story Completion Test. However, it is important to note that existing measures have not always been developed to a fully reliable level, and no universally established observational protocol exists. Measuring Attachment in Adults Two primary methods for assessing attachment in adults are the Adult Attachment Interview (AAI) and self-report questionnaires. These tools were developed with different goals in mind. According to Shaver and Fraley, self-report measures of romantic attachment and the AAI were initially created independently and for distinct purposes. Self-report questionnaires focus on a person’s feelings and behaviors in romantic or close relationships, while the AAI is designed to infer the defenses associated with an adult’s current state of mind regarding childhood relationships with parents. Although these measures might have been expected to correlate strongly, they are only moderately related as currently assessed. Each measure derives its construct validity from different domains: self-report measures from studies of romantic relationships and the AAI from predictions about a person’s child’s behavior in the Strange Situation. The AAI and self-report questionnaires provide distinct but equally valid perspectives on adult attachment, making it worthwhile to understand both approaches. Adult Attachment Interview (AAI) The AAI, developed by Mary Main and colleagues, is a semi-structured interview that takes about one hour to administer. It includes approximately 20 questions and has extensive research validation. A detailed description can be found in Chapter 19 of Attachment Theory, Research, and Clinical Applications, edited by J. Cassidy and P. R. Shaver. The chapter, titled The Adult Attachment Interview: Historical and Current Perspectives, is authored by E. Hesse. One of the strongest validations of the AAI is its ability to predict interviewees’ children’s classifications in the Strange Situation. The AAI also shows some overlap with attachment constructs measured by less time-intensive tools from the peer/romantic attachment tradition, such as those developed by Hazan and Shaver or Bartholomew. However, the AAI primarily measures a person’s state of mind regarding attachment in their family of origin rather than romantic attachment. Self-Report Questionnaires Hazan and Shaver created the first questionnaire to measure attachment in adults. This questionnaire classified adults into the three attachment styles identified by Ainsworth: secure, avoidant, and anxious/ambivalent. Participants were asked to choose which set of statements best described their feelings, with each set corresponding to an attachment style. Later versions introduced scales that allowed participants to rate how well each set of statements described their feelings. An important advancement in attachment questionnaires was the addition of a fourth attachment style. Bartholomew and Horowitz proposed a model identifying four categories of adult attachment based on individuals’ thoughts about their partners and themselves. Specifically, attachment styles depended on whether people judged their partners to be generally accessible and responsive to support requests and whether they judged themselves as individuals others would want to help. The four categories were: 1. Secure: Positive thoughts about self and partner. 2. Dismissive: Positive thoughts about self but negative thoughts about partner. 3. Preoccupied: Negative thoughts about self but positive thoughts about partner. 4. Fearful: Negative thoughts about both self and partner. Bartholomew and Horowitz used this model to create the Relationship Questionnaire (RC), which included four sets of statements describing these attachment styles. Tests demonstrated that the four attachment styles were distinct in how they related to other psychological variables, confirming that adults exhibit four attachment styles rather than three. David Schmitt and colleagues validated the Bartholomew and Horowitz attachment questionnaire across 62 cultures. The distinction between thoughts about self and thoughts about partners proved valid in nearly all cultures, although the interaction of these thoughts to form attachment styles varied somewhat across cultures. The four attachment styles also had slightly different meanings across cultures. Another significant advancement in attachment questionnaires was the use of independent items to assess attachment. Instead of asking participants to choose between sets of statements, they rated their agreement with dozens of individual statements. These ratings were combined to provide an attachment score. Popular questionnaires using this strategy include the Experiences in Close Relationships (ECR) questionnaire and its revised version (ECR-R). The ECR was created by Brennan, Clark, and Shaver in 1998, and the ECR-R was developed by Fraley, Waller, and Brennan in 2000. The ECR and ECR-R group questionnaire items into two dimensions of attachment: anxiety and avoidance. Anxiety items measure how anxious a person feels about their relationship, while avoidance items measure how avoidant they are in their relationship. Researchers often use scores from these scales for statistical analyses and hypothesis testing. Scores on the anxiety and avoidance scales can also classify individuals into the four adult attachment styles. The secure attachment style is characterized by low anxiety and low avoidance. The preoccupied style is marked by high anxiety and low avoidance. The dismissive-avoidant style is defined by low anxiety and high avoidance. Finally, the fearful-avoidant style is characterized by high anxiety and high avoidance.
